utterances.text: Did you have an opportunity to review this document when you came here, Mr. Davidovic?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did have the opportunity to see it.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And the assessment that General Mladic gives here on the paramilitaries, is that a correct assessment, according to your own observations?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not understand the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Could you please repeat your answer? The interpreters didn't hear you.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's absolutely true, the overview of the situation, and it corresponds to the actual situation.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: General Mladic also refers to their association with profiteers and authorities. In relation to Bijeljina, who would that be, the authorities and the profiteers?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The local powers, the local government, crisis staffs, and those who can work within those crisis staffs and have permission to carry out certain jobs that are outside of the jurisdiction of the army. This would be trade, the import of different articles, such as fuel, cigarettes, alcohol, other items of that nature.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Can we please have the next page in both languages. And in the B/C/S, please, the previous one.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: General Mladic orders what is supposed to happen with those kind of paramilitaries, including joining them to the regular army, arresting and disarming them, and so on and so forth. Do you know why this joint action, that was executed in July 1992 and not already earlier?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This order did yield some results, in the sense of attempting to arrest the paramilitary formation members and to place them under the command of the army. However, this was not successful for the simple reason that the paramilitary formations had the support of the local authorities, crisis staffs, certain high-ranking functionaries, and when the army opposes them and if there was a conflict, they were always then released, freed, and they would continue to do whatever they were doing. So I don't think that this order managed to create any particular results. The same thing went on until the end of the war. There were always paramilitary formations who committed different crimes, and nobody could oppose them, although I know for sure, and I'm repeating a number of times, that General Ratko Mladic was always against these paramilitary formations, but he could not confront them. He even stated that paramilitary formations were -- the Serbian Volunteer Guards and other units, that they waged war as much as they wanted, and they were protected by those whose existence suited them. So, in fact, there were no results in the sense of trying to establish command or subordinate them to the military.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Karadzic please repeat his question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You just overlapped with the interpretation. Could you repeat?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we establish whether this is the same document, because the one in the English has numbers of paragraphs which are not there in the original and I don't recognize the contents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's move to the last page, page 3.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: When you -- yes, there are the numbers. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think this is, more or less, all right now, but we didn't see the last typewritten page.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. This document is already in evidence. I would ask that Exhibit 65 ter 08106 be brought up on the screen, please. And as it is coming up: It is a report drafted by Danilo Vukovic, related to the work results, 26 June to 25th July 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Davidovic, do you know of this report?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm familiar with the document, and I am one of the drafters.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, can it be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Was that all of your question, whether ...?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: He was one of the drafters, therefore the question, Is this a correct description of what happened?, seems a bit strange, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, yes, it will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P2881, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I would ask that Exhibit 65 ter 00651 - I see it's P00036 - be brought up on the screen. It is already in evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: This report now by Mr. Dragan Andan, is that something you know from that time, and is it correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll not broadcast this.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On what basis?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we go into private session.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Just, Mr. Davidovic, what is described here about the activities, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Can we please have 65 ter 18844 be brought up on the screen. And as it is coming up: It is a document dated 8 August 1992, from the Public Prosecutor in Zvornik to the Lower Court, and charging a number of persons, including Vojin and Dusko Vuckovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Davidovic, do you know this document?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: How do you know it? Did you know it at that time already?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was interested in the proceedings against Zuco. I'm thinking of Vojin, Rade, all the others against whom charges were submitted. And when I came to the Bijeljina SUP, I asked them to show me the charges, and to see what was done about that, and why the case was not processed. And that is why I'm familiar with all the details about what happened and what the reason was for these criminal proceedings to be kept quiet about.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Davidovic, could you help us with this? It says "Public Prosecutor," and also refers to MUP. Is the Public Prosecutor subordinated to MUP?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. The MUP is a special organisation that works on uncovering crimes, and a criminal report is provided to the Office of the Prosecutor, and it is not subordinated to the MUP in any way. It is even above the MUP, in a way. And it is the Prosecutor's Office that processes all these criminal reports that are filed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The MUP is copying this report to the Public Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. We write what had happened and what the reason was for filing a criminal report, and then the Prosecutor's Office decides whether there is criminal liability or not and whether they are ultimately going to initiate proceedings or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. I now understand it. This will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P2882, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Davidovic, you spoke about Bijeljina and the Zvornik crisis staffs in your statement, and I would just want to put to you one document in this context. 65 ter 02552, can this be -- please be brought up. We would need the -- yes, yes. Can the -- yes, thank you very much. Mr. Davidovic, it is a conclusion of the Zvornik Interim Government of the 20th of April, 1992, appointing a Commission for Negotiations. These persons listed here, do you know them.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know them.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And this Ljubisa Mauzer, it's called "Mauzer" here, he is from Bijeljina or not?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He's from Bijeljina. You can see here the conclusion of the provisional government. When Arkan came to Bijeljina with a group of his warriors, or members of his unit, when he went to Zvornik, he took along some people from Bijeljina as well who, at the time when Arkan had a training camp on the Drina River, he took along those people as well, who joined him to attack or, rather, liberate Zvornik. A large number of group -- a large group of Muslims in Zvornik wanted to move towards Tuzla. They were asking to be allowed, irrespective of all the movable and immovable property they had, to be allowed to leave. And I'm sure that this commission was established with the intention of negotiating. I'm surprised to see Ljubisa Mauzer -- Ljubisa Savic, nicknamed Mauzer, on this commission when he's not from the area of Zvornik and he has nothing to do with it. He just happened to be there, and, well, he was this military leader who, if I can put it that way, was supposed to help the government in Zvornik to deal with this more easily.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, can this be admitted, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A question, please. It would be a good thing if we had a signed copy with a stamp, or if, as it says here, it was published in the bulletin of the Serb Municipality, then its authenticity could not be denied, and even more so because "Savic" is the last name of Ljubisa Savic. "Mauzer" is only his nickname.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, we can check for this, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't follow his last. What about Savic? Could you -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, number 2 there, "Ljubisa Mauzer," the person's actual name is "Savic," and "Mauzer" is like a nickname, and so he's questioning why an official document would include a nickname of an individual, and that has some bearing on its authenticity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I know that all goes to the matter of weight, which can be explored in his cross-examination. We'll admit this and move on.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P2883, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Can we please have 65 ter 07346 be brought up. And it actually relates to the man, Mauzer. It's an interview with Mauzer on 15 June 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Davidovic, did you have an opportunity to read this interview during your preparations?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: What kind of this publication is this: "List SAO Semberije i Majevice"?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a paper that was being issued by the Crisis Staff of Bijeljina. In actual fact, it was supposed to cover the territory of the newly-formed SAO Majevica and Semberija. In the area of Republika Srpska, well, as they say, there are different regions that it's being divided up into, SAO, MAO, et cetera, and then they get their own regions, Semberija and Majevica. So it's Bijeljina, Brcko, Lopare, Ugljevik, Zvornik, and more or less all of that up to Bratunac and Srebrenica, Sekovici, Milici, all of those locations in that part of Bosnia. And these are special defence preparations.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Is there a -- what do you mean, that these are special defence preparations? What do you mean by saying this?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I say "defence preparations," a civil war was in the making. It was obvious, it seemed inevitable. All of that could be seen from what the politicians were saying and what the media were saying. They said -- they kept on saying that there would be a war, inevitably that would be --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the end.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] ... unless certain agreements were to be reached, and they never seemed to be able to reach these agreements.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: The interpreters didn't get a part of your answer. It is here stated: "They kept on saying that there would be a war, inevitable that would be ..." And then they lost you. Could you complete the answer?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would be hard, a difficult war.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Davidovic, do you know this journalist, Pero Simic?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know him well, I know him well. He was the editor of this Semberija newspaper, and he was one of the initiators of this misinformation in the territory of Semberija. It wasn't only him, but he was one of the key persons there. They called him a small-scale Goebbels.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And when you say "misinformation," what do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The untruths that were presented in these newspapers. Different things were being written there; for example, some Muslims who lived in Bijeljina, prominent Muslims, people I knew, that allegedly now they joined the Muslim military formations and that they were taking people into war, and that at Majevica they had established lines that were supposed to be taken, and that actually they were in charge of this war, that they were waging this war. All of this was preconceived in order to attain the desired objective to sow fear, panic, uncertainty for something that would be inevitable, and that is the war that would follow. Then in the media, they came up with these violent programmes, propaganda, various wrong news, like the ones I mentioned to you now, and then also patriotic songs, Chetnik songs, Get ready, Chetniks, we are going to slaughter all those who don't wish to join us. All of this was supposed to show that we would not allow ourselves to lose the war that would inevitably follow.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Davidovic, when you look at the first page here, Mr. Savic, Mauzer, speaks of Bijeljina, a peaceful and normal life, and he speaks -- he says this in mid-1992. Is that -- was there a normal and peaceful life at that time?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, no. He's saying that it's a peaceful town, and he's talking about people moving out and population exchanges. How can it be a peaceful town when one-third of the Muslim population had already left, or was expelled, and others were being expelled and taken out during the night and taken to the separation lines? He thinks that it's a peaceful town because they are keeping silent and obediently following orders, without resisting what they are being told. Rather, they take this docile attitude and simply obey whatever they're asked to do.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And can we look at the -- in the English, it must be now the second page. The B/C/S is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: We have here Mauzer speaking of a large enclave of Muslims living and working normally. Is that a correct description or not?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that is not correct. This is a total lie. What it says here is incorrect, and they are trying to present before the public a picture that is wrong, saying that everything is peaceful and that all is well. I can give you a few details that are important, in terms of what was going on in Bijeljina at the time, what was happening to the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, but very briefly, because we have quite an extensive statement to this effect.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very briefly. The Muslims were being called upon to respond to the military call-up through military departments, to be members of the Army of Republika Srpska. When they refused that, then these Muslims are immediately laid off, not able to work any longer. They're telephones are being disconnected, and those who oppose this publicly or suggest to their other compatriots who are also Muslims to do that, then they take them to Batkovici. As for Muslims who cannot go to Tuzla, or if they don't have enough money to pay for this and money is being taken for their alleged exchange, then attempts are made for eminent Muslims, all of those who are educated, who are intellectuals, they are humiliated so that they would see what their place is then; for example, the principal of the music school or, for example, the previous deputy from the SUP, then the director of the construction company, Rad, then Dr. Jahija. And many others, who were leading intellectuals, were being engaged to sweep the streets. They were simply trying to show them what their place is. Can you imagine a doctor, a pediatrician, who is being sent to the market with a little bag, or a director of the music school, swearing a suit and a tie, who is sweeping the street? Can you imagine what effect this has on the Muslims? When he says that the situation is fine, that is what was actually happening.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like to have a video-clip played, and I really hope it works now. 65 ter 40578, and we play the section 00:49 -- 49:40 to 00:52:30.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "This is one of the many new admission centres in Tuzla, last night, one hour before midnight. Following the 1400 expelled Bosniaks from Semberija who were accommodated in the other admission centres in Tuzla and the neighbouring towns yesterday, soon this hall will be prepared to admit new victims, who will come in the course of the night from Mount Majevica area. It is midnight. Bus after bus is arriving to Tuzla during this rainy and chilly night. Those who are coming are women, children, old people, and only now and then a man fit for military service. Others have been separated from their families by Chetnik gangs and imprisoned in camps. There are Bosniak families arriving, who were once well off but now all their property has been seized and looted, and who even had to pay a lot in foreign currency and gold for deportation tickets, for night walk in rain and through Majevica woods, past minefields. Even seriously disabled, poor old grannies, and paralysed Munevera Bajramovic. Hopefully at least someone in this dormant world will ask to whom had Munevera Bajramovic posed an threat, same as Zade Manjic's twins, also from Janja. They don't even have names yet, they're just born, yet these days the brother and sister from Manjic family will get border passes and number for toddlers. Lord, may in Bosnia justice prevail at last. These people are not handball or basketball game spectators, these people are expelled Bosniaks from Janja waiting for mattresses and sponges to be pulled down on the hall floor - the ill fate and constant companions of Bosniaks in the current days of horrible genocide committed against them by Chetnik military leaders from Pale. "People are waiting. Another Tuzla admission centre hall is slowing filling up. The second hour past midnight is passing. This night another 427 expellees have arrived from Semberija. The people with terrible scars on their soul, physically and emotionally broken. The only thing that criminals at least spent peacefully -- they're getting ready to at least spend peacefully their second night in exile. The first night, they spent surrounded by gangs of Vojkan Djurkovic, Rista, and other war criminals in the trucks on Majevica Mountain. It is the 19th of September of the war year 1994. Tuzla, one hour past noon, yet another bus from Majevica and yet another group of Bosniak expellees. The Janja tragedy is getting to an end, and now its turn for final ethnic cleansing of Bijeljina, while the world is still talking about the dictators from Haiti."

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Davidovic, did you have an opportunity to see this footage?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: During the events, were you aware about the forcible removal of non-Serbs from Janja in September 1994?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I did know about that, of course. How could I not know about that? I lived there with my family. I came there every weekend when I was not in Belgrade. Every day, I asked people what was going on and where the end would be. First, Bijeljina was done. 80 per cent of the Muslims had already been taken out of the town of Bijeljina. And then in September, they moved on to Janja. Janja tried to hang on. They even tried to feed the Army of Republika Srpska. After all, these are hard-working farmers who can provide lots of food. But even that could not help. Quite simply, their turn had to come, I mean, their turn to be transferred to other parts of -- from Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And what is described in the video, the way that this was done, is that what you -- is that consistent with what you also observed or got to know?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, yes. This was a time-tested method. Lists were made, and these lists were being given to Vojkan Djurkovic. At the time, the police was withdrawing from the streets. No one dared oppose him. He went from house to house, knowing which houses belonged to Muslims, and he took people out of their houses, took them into trucks. What do you think? What can you do when they give you a ten-minute dead-line to leave your house and everything you have? What did people take? They take their personal IDs, they take their diplomas, if any, a bit of clothes, and money or other valuables they have. When they gather 300, 400, or even more than that, they take them to Suvo Polje. That is where they put them up, search them in great detail. I have to admit that even old women were subjected to gynaecological examinations, women of over 80 years of age. They were looking for money wherever they could. When they get all of that, then they put them onto buses or trucks or -- and then take them to Brcko or Majevica, to the separation line. They let them leave the trucks from the Serb side, and then they go towards Muslim territory. And what happened then was that the Muslims would not take them in immediately either, because sometimes this happened late at night, so they waited until dawn to see who these people were. So when these people were being expelled or deported from Republika Srpska, they would spend a night or a day or two or three in no-man's land, and then they would finally get through and be taken in by the Muslims. And that is how families were reunited. Also, there were cases of organised transfers through the MUP, going through Serbia, and then they were taken in the same way. They were taken to the army between -- at the border with Hungary. The Hungarians would not take them, and then after a few days the International Red Cross would come and get them and take them to other European countries. That happened on a daily basis from the beginning of April, then May, June, until the end of the war.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Davidovic. Can we have -- can this be admitted, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, this will be admitted. But you are not minded to tender the interview with Mauzer into evidence?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. I forgot.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Any observation, Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Both will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter 07346 shall be Exhibit P2884, and the video will be Exhibit P2885, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Can we please have 65 ter 00625 be brought up on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And as it is coming up, Mr. Davidovic, we have already referred to people being moved out via Serbia, and what we have here is an interview with Marko Pavlovic, dated the 30th of June, 1992, to the -- to "Borba" in Belgrade. Did you have an opportunity to read this article in preparation of your testimony?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Pavlovic is speaking about the situation in Kozluk and the wider area, and is speaking of the massive moving out of Muslims, and he says that he would not know why they want to leave, given their freedom of movement. Did you know about this moving out in summer 1992 of quite a huge number of people from Zvornik; in particular, Kozluk?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I did know that from the area of Kozluk, they had picked up all the Muslims and reached some kind of agreement there allowing them to go unhindered via Serbia, not to Europe, but, as they said, to reunite with their families. So the people from Kozluk, led by Banjanovic at the time - he was an assemblyman who was some kind of leader of theirs - they were given some kind of consent to go from Kozluk to Zvornik, and then they put them all up at the dom in Celopek. In Celopek, they were taken by the reserve police in accordance with the decision of the Crisis Staff. They were securing this building in Celopek. And then when I went to arrest the Yellow Wasps, I had an opportunity of seeing armed persons standing by the Dom. I didn't know that these people persons were there at the time. It was only later that I heard that these persons were put up there and later transferred somewhere towards Europe or the Federation. I don't know how they left the premises. I heard that in that building, some persons were even taken out and killed by Zuco's members, especially some journalist of the "Duga" weekly, which was particularly very brutal. He did horrible things to people there. He cut off their ears and --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Davidovic, let's stay with the people from Kozluk that were moving out. Mr. Pavlovic says here that they -- they left voluntarily and they exchanged their houses. Did the Muslims leave voluntarily?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Who could they exchange their houses with? How come? Who -- whoever is a normal person, we all have our homes and our families. Who will say, of his own free will, I'm going to hand all of this over, this is where I live, this is where my nearest and dearest were buried, my ancestors? How are they going to say, We voluntarily want to leave this area? People were saving their lives. Let's try to survive. We are offering everything to you, our houses, our movable and immovable property. We're giving you everything. Just let us live, and let us reunite with our families, and let us leave this area. So people just tried to leave this hell, one way or the other, because they had no other way out. That is why they left all their property. They voluntarily handed it over to the Serb Army and everyone else, and then they just left. What reasonable person would want to leave everything that they had earned over the years, or even the previous generations, too? Am I clear when I say all of this?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, definitely. Mr. Davidovic, what we also find in this article, and it's a little bit further down in the English, Mr. Pavlovic states that it would be best for the people to be moved into enclaves, for the properties to be exchanged, and for these enclaves to be nationally homogenised so that at least temporarily there are as few nationally-mixed places. What Mr. Pavlovic is saying here, did you hear these kind of views expressed by others as well?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Pavlovic is saying what the Crisis Staff and the politicians expect him to say. You shouldn't think it's up to an individual, that it's all the responsibility of this Marko Pavlovic. He just came from the outside and placed himself at the disposal of the Crisis Staff to implement policies they had charted. I can say with certainty that it was the policy of the SDS to have the Muslims moved out. It was not only in Brcko or Bijeljina or Zvornik. It was not even their decision. That happened in every area of Republika Srpska wherever the SDS was in power. It was a planned operation. It could not have happened spontaneously in such an identical way everywhere. The Crisis Staff did nothing more or other than putting in place the instructions they had been given. It's not a coincidence; it was a rule.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would request the admission of this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P2886, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I note the time. It's time to have a break, if it is convenient.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll have a break for an hour and resume at 1.30. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.33 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Can we please have 65 ter 645 on the screen. And as it is coming up: It is a newspaper article in the newspaper "The Independent," dated the 19th of July, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Davidovic, did you have an opportunity to read this article when you prepared for the testimony?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you allow me just to read it. Yes, I've seen it, yes. I'm sorry, I wasn't seeing it right from the beginning.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Can we please have the second page in English and the third page in the B/C/S, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: On the top of the page in the B/C/S, and rather further down, second-last paragraph in the English, there's reference to Mr. Banjanovic, and you mentioned him already, that he took part in this removal of the Muslim population in Kozluk. What role did he actually have in it?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, he was an activist earlier, either of the Socialist Alliance or some other organisation in Kozluk, and he did have a certain influence on the inhabitants of Kozluk. He was their ideological leader. He participated in negotiations in Kozluk. They contacted him. I know Pavlovic told me that he was sorry he didn't kill him. It's a no-good man who cheated everybody and escaped. And the Muslims, nevertheless, managed to leave, thanks to him, and to pull out with as few losses as possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And Mr. Banjanovic states here that he told the villagers, on the 25th of June, that they had only one hour to get ready to leave, and that they faced only two options: to flee or to stay and be killed. Mr. Davidovic, in relation to your own observations, were these the options that the Muslim villagers had?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They were given an hour, and even that is a lot. So he still managed to get an hour. Otherwise, usually when Vojkan Djurkovic was assembling people, then he would give 10, 15 minutes at the most. This time, they were given an hour, in their version. Yeah, it's a lot.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Davidovic, I would like now to move on to Brcko, and for this I would like to have Exhibit 65 ter 07113 be brought up on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And you are tendering this "Independent" article?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Sorry. Yes, I forgot. Yes, I would like to tender it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P2887, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Davidovic, it is a summary of events and situations, with an assessment of the degree of achievement, related to Brcko. Did you have -- did you have the opportunity to review this document in preparation of your testimony?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Were you aware of this document during the events in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I came to Brcko in 1992, the Crisis Staff informed me about this review of events in order for me to be able to get into the problem more easily.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And if we please look at the last page in the B/C/S, and the same in the English. No, sorry, not the last page; the second-last page in the B/C/S, the previous one. The English, it should be the last page, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Davidovic, who is signing this report?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who could have signed it. I'm not familiar with the signatures. But I assume that it was Beli. He was the deputy -- he was the president of the Brcko Crisis Staff. He was a deputy. They called him "Beli," I called him "Beli." He was a deputy in the Republican Assembly of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And this document has no date on it. When did you get this information during the events, so that we can narrow it down a bit?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: May/June 1992, in late May or early June.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Can we please have page 1 in the English and page 2 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: In the second paragraph in the B/C/S, and in the third paragraph from the bottom, there is a -- there is a reference that there is a threat to the Serbian population in the municipality. Knowing the area, do you know whether there was such a threat and what this threat was?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In view of the overall situation before the war in Brcko, the ethnic structure was as follows: The Muslims were the most numerous, followed by the Serbs and then the Croats. Since the Muslim and the Croat sides were linked up, they felt that they were endangered. And in view of the proximity of Croatia, they felt that they were in an unfavorable situation. And because of that, they felt that they were in danger and that they needed help, and that was the reason why they asked for help from the Crisis Staff in Bijeljina. And that assistance was given.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Can we please have page 3 in the English and page 5 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: There is -- on this page, there is a reference and a description of the various troops arriving to help out in Brcko, and there is also reference to Semberija and the two formations; in particular, those of Mauzer and those of Mirko Blagojevic. Do you know whether forces from Bijeljina participated in the events in Brcko, and which?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As it happened, I was in Bijeljina when Bijeljina and the Crisis Staff were preparing to extend assistance for the liberation of Brcko. And I say "liberation" in quotes. I was in a commission in Croatia, and then I got some days off, so it was either before or after or on the 1st of May, that holiday, very likely that it happened in that period. I went to town, and it just happened that I met -- or I encountered a large gathering of people on the square. I could see uniformed units arriving, also members of the active and reserve police forces, soldiers, members of the military reserve who had been mobilised that day. I could see that the people who were coming were running to the reporting place, taking the most basic things with them, carrying the summonses in their hand to report to somebody. I could see that the person in charge there was Mauzer, with a bullhorn, and the Crisis Staff leadership from Bijeljina was next to him. Dr. Novakovic was there as well, Milan Novakovic, the president of the SDS, deputy, all of those who were persons who counted in Bijeljina, if I can put it like that. Arkan's people were there, Pejo, Sasa. Legija was there, many of those whom I knew from Belgrade from the police. People were wearing police uniforms. A number of Arkan's men were wearing police uniforms with the insignia of chief inspectors even though that is not a rank that they ever held. There were interesting details there that I was interested in. What's going on, I asked. What is this, what sort of review is this? They said, well, they're getting ready to go to Brcko to liberate it. I said, From whom? They said, Well, there are Muslims and Croats over there, the said, so that the people from Bijeljina can finish this whole thing up. Before they set off, I could see that they were all lined up on the square, and they made a solemn oath. All of them were crossing themselves. Those who had not been baptised and were Orthodox were given the opportunity to be baptised. There was a priest there. I told him -- I told him, What are you doing? I'm not familiar with these terms; I'm an atheist. So the priest was baptising everybody. And among the members of the active police there were Muslims, there were people whom I knew, subordinate policemen. I had known them from before. I was a superior officer of that organ, so, more or less, I knew all of those people. Some of them noticed me, but I was standing to the side, near the courthouse, near a corner. I didn't want to be too obvious. After the line-up was finished, they entered trucks and buses, and they were going in to go and liberate Brcko. It's a paradox, it's an interesting piece of information. They were followed by about 100 small TAM trucks. These trucks were following them. Later, I found out that after Brcko was liberated, lots of things were taken and piled into all of those trucks and brought back after the action to liberate Brcko was over.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we have this document admitted, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P2888, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I would now ask Exhibit 65 ter 07711 be brought up on the screen. And as it is coming up: It's an extraordinary report of the East Bosnia Corps, chief of intelligence organ, of the VRS Main Staff -- sorry, to the chief of the VRS Main Staff, of 29 September 1992. Mr. Davidovic, did you have an opportunity to review this document in the preparation for your testimony?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: This document is -- originates from a Captain Simeon Guduric [phoen]. Do you know this person?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just by name in passing. I never had any direct contacts with him.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: In the bigger paragraph on the first page, he states that the town was flooded with different patriotic-oriented individuals, who used devotion to Serbism as an excuse for robberies, rapes and murders, and he also refers to his belief that group had support of the then military and civilian authorities. Would that be a correct assessment or not?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, quite correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, can we have this document admitted, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P2889, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I forgot to ask you something in relation to this document. In this document, there's also a reference to murders in Luka. Were you aware of the Camp Luka and who was detained there?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before I came to Brcko, I was informed at the Crisis Staff that there was a group of people detained in Luka. According to the same system, in order to achieve full control over the Muslims, there was a kind of labour camp which served to place those who were undesirable there; mostly Muslims. Before I came, I heard that individuals would barge into the camp in Luka, where they were liquidating people. I heard that this was done by the Red Berets and another paramilitary organisation, Bozic brothers. All of these groups felt they had the right to do the things that are stated in this report. When we came, I will say that when we entered Brcko, when we took over the internal affairs organ, the municipality and other institutions, we went to the Luka, in Brcko - it was after midnight, 2.00, 3.00 a.m. - and we found about 60 detainees. Among them, there were children. I ordered the doors of the hangars to be opened. People came out. It was night, it was nightmarish. People didn't know what was going on. There was shooting from all sides, and nobody believed it. It was night. There was firing. In order to say who I am, I said, I am the legal government. What does it mean at that point in time, to say that I am the legal authority, legal government? It means that I'm an active police officer, that I am speaking, stating my first and last name, talking about the police representing the legal state. I said that it was war, that people should flee, they should hide, because when they leave here, I cannot guarantee their safety, and let them do the best they can to find some safe shelter. After half an hour, nobody was there anymore. They had all gone. I assumed they went to their friends', acquaintances'. I don't know where they managed to go. In any case, we set a curfew. There was no more moving around. There were no more arbitrary arrests. I didn't see the people who were in Luka at the time, but later I had people coming up to me after the fact and thanking me.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Davidovic, just one other camp I would like to speak to you about, and that's the Batkovic Camp. And you have spoken about it already, and also in your written statement, you have information about that. Can we please have 65 ter 11292 be brought up on the screen. Mr. Davidovic, it is an order of the 2nd of July, 1992, of the East Bosnia Corps Command to establish a camp. Do you know which camp that relates to?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I read the order. It pertains to the Batkovic Camp. I think at the time the proposal originated from Dencic. Later, it was taken up by Colonel Ilic. And then they went to implement it, to ask the municipality for an area where they could have a collection centre or, as they described it, some kind of labour camp. Later, it turned into a real camp. And then they were offered a space in Batkovic by the Semberija enterprise, where there was some hangars and stables, hangars to place the equipment in and the stables or the barns for the livestock.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters note: We did not hear the last sentence by the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Davidovic, could you please repeat the last sentence, because the interpreters couldn't hear that.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To form the camp there, if that's what they mean.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Davidovic, here we have the date 2nd of July, 1992. When did the camp start operating, or do you know that?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They began preparing it a little bit earlier. It took some time to get the space, to build the fence, to build the doors, to create the minimum of conditions in order to be able to place people there, so it took some time before the camp began to work officially.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And who was the first camp commander? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. Milos, Marko. Milos, Despot's son. His name is Marko. He lived in Nis, but he came from the Command of the Federal Secretariat of National Defence. He transferred there, and then he was given the assignment of forming a camp. And he was among the first of those to write the decree order, manner and instructions on how to maintain order, discipline and responsibility in the camp. I just happened to know this man, and only after the war I heard from him. He said he was the commander of the camp. I couldn't believe it. He told me some details here, and actually when I came here, I just happened to see a document with his signature. He was there very briefly, for a month. After that, he had to return to Nis because of a family tragedy, and then he never returned.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, can this document be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P2890, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And as you just mentioned it, can we please have Exhibit 11777 pulled up on the screen. Mr. Davidovic, is that the document that you were just referring to having seen?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's the instruction for security commanders.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And can we have the last page of the document in both languages.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Is that -- what we see here, the person signing, is that the gentleman that you referred to earlier?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P2891, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You mentioned, in your amalgamated statement, several persons that were taken to the camp. Did you also manage to get someone released from the camp?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never went to Batkovic. I wanted to have nothing to do with it, and I didn't want my unit to have anything to do with it. However, when I returned from Bosnia to the Federal Secretariat for the Interior, Minister Bulatovic asked me, privately and officially, to try and find one person there. He was an electrical engineer, that man. I was given his name, Karakaj [phoen]. And Minister Bulatovic asked me to look for that person. He had some vague reports that he might be in Batkovic. So the first chance I got, I went to Bijeljina for a weekend to see if that man was there and if I could reach him. I went to Suvo Polje, where the corps command was located. I found the corps commander, Colonel Ilic, and told him about my errand. I must say I was on very good terms with Colonel Ilic, because in my position for the Federal Secretariat for the Interior, I had helped him earlier arrange some of his business. So I made the request to look for that person, and if he's found, that be released and allowed to go to Serbia for a family reunion. And he said, That will be done. I will be given news, if any, and I be able to take that person with me. So I came the next day, around 3.00 or 4.00 p.m. I found Colonel Ilic there. The man had already been brought there. That was the first time I saw him, and they just gave him to me. I didn't even have to sign a paper or anything. I took that person to my home, gave him a change of clothes, told him to have a shower, gave him my clothes, and that night I took him to Belgrade. I had no problems crossing the border because I was wearing a uniform and I was never checked at the border because everybody knew me, more or less. So that same night, I was in Belgrade. I called Minister Bulatovic to tell him that that the man he had wanted to see was in Belgrade. I took him to Bulatovic's apartment. I was told that his family had come to pick him up a few days later. I never heard any more about it. But if you need to know, I can try to find out and let you know later. That's the one occasion when I helped to get someone out of there.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Davidovic. Your Honour, this concludes the examination-in-chief. However, there is the request to also admit the associated exhibits. And I know Mr. Robinson mentioned, in the very beginning, that he would not want the exhibits that are listed in footnote 144 be admitted. That's my understanding. The Prosecution wishes to tender these statements that are mentioned in this footnote, for a variety of reasons. First of all, these documents confirm what the witness is stating in his amalgamated statement, as he describes the arrest scenario of the Yellow Wasps. He describes how they were arrested, how statements were taken from them, and how it then developed. The documents confirm the number of people arrested, quite a number of persons, their names, names that come up also on the various lists that we have discussed here in court. We could see these names. We could see the dates when the statements were taken. We could see that the statements are focusing on the group -- on the person's group affiliation, being the Yellow Wasps and also others, and they also relate to car theft and the confiscation of other goods, including also those confiscated from RS officials that happened to come across these barricades that were managed by the Yellow Wasps. Therefore, I think it confirms the witness's evidence, it confirms procedure. And, therefore, I would like to have these statements also accepted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Those are all that are in footnote 144?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, these are the ones in 144, and I address them only because I know that Mr. Robinson did not want this to be accepted. Of course, we also want all other -- all other associated exhibits admitted, and they are all described in details in the amalgamated statement. They are listed in our submission -- our notification. Some of them we have already addressed today here, but most of them not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Can I hear from you, Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. President. First of all, we don't object to the associated exhibits, except for the 14 statements. The reason we object to those is: First of all, everything that Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff said is true about their contents, but, nevertheless, you haven't been admitting statements of third parties, and there's a good reason for that. Number 1, it detracts from our ability to have effective confrontation of witnesses providing information to the Chamber. And, secondly, it subverts Rule 92 bis, which is the proper way for the Prosecution or any party to take a statement of a witness and have it subject to the certification process, and then seek to have it admitted. So to admit statements of third parties under these circumstances as associated exhibits we don't believe is proper, and we ask that you not admit them. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. President, but if I -- if the Court would permit me just to respond quickly, because I have been present during the course of discussions about statements and whether they should be admitted or not. I just want to underscore I think this is a horse of another colour. There's no effort here to subvert 92 bis or a suggestion that swallows the Rule. It's a different matter. Here, we're talking about an investigation under issue, what was investigated, what was the focus of the investigation, what information was obtained, what action was taken or not taken in response to that, and that presents a different matter. And that's why the Prosecution is offering them in this instance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll admit everything except for those 14 statements, and also that has not been yet tendered. And then we'll consider the admission of those 14 matters and issue our decision -- give our decision in due course. Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic. Mr. Davidovic, you will be further asked by Mr. Karadzic in his cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Good afternoon to everyone. At the outset, I want to apologise to the interpreters because we will produce a few documents that have not been translated. We made a priority list last week and sent it to the CLSS, but not all of these documents have yet been translated. So I ask for your understanding.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Davidovic.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, such a simple statement cannot be an excuse for not having prepared an English translation. So I'll give you this warning again, and do your best. We'll see how many untranslated documents you are going to present. But if necessary, we will revisit the issue. On a separate matter, we, the Chamber, took a look at the Exhibit P36, which was put under seal, but we don't see the need to keep it under seal. So --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We are minded to lift --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Yes. Yes, because also this document, itself, does not refer to the protected witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That will be done. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With your leave, Your Excellency, it is the CLSS that is over-worked and over-loaded. We have done our bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Davidovic, can you tell us when you had your first contact with this Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember exactly, but it must have been four or five years ago, maybe more.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: At whose initiative?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the request of the OTP of the Tribunal in The Hague.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I must remind you that we are speaking the same language, so we need to make a pause between question and answer. The same applies to me, and I will probably err in this respect myself. What was your status then? Have you ever had the status of witness -- suspect, and until when?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was never a suspect. I was never investigated or interrogated in any case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it correct that you are testifying here both about things you have seen or heard at the time there, or a long time later, and things that you have learned from the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, before this Court, I am talking only about things that I did myself, that I saw myself, and that I learnt in direct contact with people as a police officer while gathering information that I needed just because I needed to inform my superiors. And I also had a personal interest in the things that were going on and the situation that came to prevail in the area of Republika Srpska because I was born there, I lived my life there. And until a year before the war started, I was one of the highest-ranking officers in Bijeljina. And let me add that nobody taught me, especially not the Prosecution, what I should say. I am not such a pliable man that I could be led to say anything anyone wants.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So you have not testified about things that you heard as rumours and gossip, and you have not testified about things that you first learned about from the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I testified about the things that I've already stated. And I also gave my comments about certain documents that were shown to me, specifying whether I had seen them before or it was the first time I was seeing them. I answered all the questions on that basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Earlier today, you mentioned that you realised certain things in the beginning of May. Is it right that at the request of the leadership of Republika Srpska - let me not mention my own contacts with Prime Minister Panic - you came to Republika Srpska on the 26th of June on an assignment to help the police force of Republika Srpska to deal with the problem of illegal armed paramilitary groups?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I was summoned by my superiors, primarily the minister of the interior, Bogdanovic, we went together to the office of General Petar Gracanin, who was minister of defence, and I was told then that they designated me to go to Republika Srpska in Bosnia and Herzegovina and to help the Ministry of Interior of Republika Srpska to disarm paramilitary units, because allegedly you, together with Prime Minister Panic of Serbia, at some meeting in Geneva or somewhere, had asked Serbia's assistance in disarming the paramilitary units in Republika Srpska, saying that you could not do it yourself, on your own, and that you needed help. So they designated that help to be me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You got 15 men then, and you came to Republika Srpska and made contact with the MUP of Republika Srpska; right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Then you were very much involved in clearing up the situation with illegal armed groups in Bijeljina, and then after that in Zvornik and Brcko, to considerable effect and results, mass arrests and elimination of these groups?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's all correct, except that Brcko came before Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You mean just the order, the sequence of municipalities?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: While you were doing that, you were receiving expressions of gratitude and recognition by the leadership; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In part, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When you over-stepped your authority, both in terms of real jurisdiction and in terms of the degree of using force, and when you got involved in some financial wrong-doing, that was the first time you were removed from the service; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not right. What you're saying has nothing to do with reality.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you continue to be involved in fraud and financial wrong-doing even after the war?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not true. You are saying rubbish.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D3645.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did the Lower Court in Bijeljina initiate a request to conduct an investigation against you and a group of other people, wherein you would be the first accused?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After I first testified in The Hague in the case of Mr. Krajisnik - I testified as a Prosecution witness - three criminal cases were started against me; not only the one you are showing, but another two. In fact, four in total. They tried, among other things, to convict me for crimes like fraud and violent behaviour. All these cases were stopped, terminated, some on the lower level, some at the level of the Higher Court. One went to appeal, and the appeal reversed the trial judgement. I kept all these judgements and I have them with me, and if the Court wants to see them, I'm happy to provide them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, according to the Public Prosecutor, the state wants to issue an indictment against this man called Mico?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is not about theft or a crime. It's about alleged over-stepping of authority, because as chairman of the Executive Board, I allowed that one apartment, owned by a certain company which was turned into a squat -- I gave authority for forcible entry so that the apartment can be evacuated.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see the last page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: When did this happen?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember correctly, but we can see it in the paper. Let's look at the date. I really can't see.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: When did the incident happen, not the proposal to issue an indictment?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It could have been in 2004, not later.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the last page. Can we see the middle page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is the proposal to indict and to schedule a trial hearing, and point 4 says: "To procure information about financial situation and criminal records for all the accused." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll mark it for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As MFI D1401, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: A month after this, on the 21st of March, 2005, did you assign or transfer a considerable amount of your property to your daughter?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not assign it. It was a sale contract whereby she bought my property. And the reason was that the money to re-purchase the apartment I got from my employer came from her in the first place. It was a sales contract that included the real value of the property.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If I understood correctly, she gave you the money to buy shares in a state-owned company or -- a state-owned company, and then you were returning the money to her?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: She had no guarantee that I would repay that money. And her husband wanted a guarantee, and that's why he asked that a sales contract be made to protect her property. I did not re-assign it to her just to cover up something.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Davidovic, if I could ask you again to put a pause between your start of answering the question of Mr. Karadzic. That way, the interpreters will be very much benefitted. Thank you for your understanding. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D3638, please, in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is a Land Registry excerpt, or a copy of it; right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see page 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is a contract on sale of real estate concluded in Bijeljina on 21 March, 1995, between Milorad Davidovic and Natasa Eric, daughter of Milorad from Bijeljina. Is that you and your daughter?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: "The seller hereby sells to the buyer the entire real estate entered in the ..." And so on and so forth?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So a month after the Prosecution requested information on your financial status, you sell to your daughter all the real estate that you owned and that was registered under these numbers; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us look at point 3: "The seller hereby states that the buyer has paid in full the amount of 429.871 convertible marks before signing this contract as the selling price ..."?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And could you read on?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: " ... and therefore agrees and allows the buyer, on the basis of this contract, without his further knowledge or permission, to register ownership over the aforementioned plots of land as owner or occupant with 1/1 share"?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I just give a comment in this regard?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As for comments, please give us a gift to Madam --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I will hear from you, Mr. Davidovic. How is this relevant, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellency, Mr. Davidovic said that he was not involved in any kind of financial wrong-doing and that he is not guilty of any such thing, but he actually accused tens of persons and smeared their names. It is very important, for the benefit of these people, to know who it is that is smearing their good names, and also this is important for his credibility as well as the reason for his dismissal from the service.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Then you should allow him to comment on this. Yes, Mr. Davidovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The criminal report that was filed against me in relation to the order or decision of the board that I presided over has to do with the entry into an apartment of a person who is not the owner. The company was the construction company Rad. This is before this purchase contract was signed. Mr. Karadzic is trying to portray me as an unreliable witness whose -- or, rather, a person who is undeserving and who does not tell the truth. As for this wrong-doing that the Prosecutor accused me of, it is only a fine that is levied, and that is, indeed, what the Court did. The Court was -- levied the fine of 500 marks, and that has nothing to do with my property, or any attempt on my part to conceal the property I had, or that would prevent the Court from disposing of my property and so on. These are completely different things. This is a minor misdemeanor that is being portrayed as some kind of grave crime. Mr. Karadzic is saying that I tried to conceal the property that I had, and I think that that is in poor taste. Secondly, after I testified as a Prosecution witness in the case against Mr. Krajisnik, I had very serious problems and suffered very serious consequences because of that testimony. Rest assured that I'm going to have some grave problems once this testimony is completed too. A lot of these people still hold high offices and decide on important matters, especially because in Bijeljina, where I live, the SDS -- from the very outset, from the beginning of the war in 1991 -- or, rather, 1992, the SDS was always in power, and these persons have a great deal of power. Ever since I appeared in court in the case against Mr. Krajisnik and in the case of Mr. Stanisic, they are trying to cast me in a negative light and as a person who was involved in different kinds of wrong-doing. I claim, with full responsibility, that I do not have a criminal record at all. I have the relevant decision in this case that he referred to. As for him saying that I had smeared the good names of tens of persons, I think that that is highly tendentious, and I kindly ask the Trial Chamber to prevent this kind of exchange from taking place between Mr. Karadzic and myself. Secondly, I'm not a person who was dismissed from the service, as he had put it. I was not dismissed from the service. I was pensioned off, along with an appropriate decision, and the decision to pension me off was based on my protection of and assistance to Muslims, and that is contained in these documents. And in my apartment in Belgrade, I kept a man, a Muslim --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not catch the name.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] ... and the SDS and the police of Republika Srpska, especially from the MUP of Bijeljina, when I left. It's not when I was dismissed, as Mr. Karadzic said. In my apartment, I was keeping this Muslim. And in the Krajisnik case, the Trial Chamber looked at the entire situation, and even during the break the OTP was in Tuzla and they talked to the direct witnesses. I retired because I had legal grounds for that and I had met all the legal requirements. I am not ashamed of anything I did. If that was the reason why I retired, then I say that with pride, that I protected this man. I did not come here as a protected witness. I came here to tell the truth. What I'm saying are serious allegations. I'm sorry, but this is the painful truth, and that is the most painful of all. Mr. Karadzic, I am a Serb, a member of the Serb people - my father, my mother, my wife - and I do not allow you to impute things of this nature to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Davidovic, thank you very much, but please understand this is a criminal proceedings and Mr. Radovan Karadzic, as an accused who is confronting serious charges, has every right to cross-examine a witness and attack the credibility. So as a Presiding Judge in charge of conducting proceedings, we'll monitor that he should not abuse the proceedings. But as far as the Chamber allows, please try to answer the question as much as you can. Do you understand, Mr. Davidovic? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, thank you. I've understood everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Davidovic, I want to get to the truth. All of us here should get to the truth together. And you said a moment ago that you say, with full responsibility, that your difficulties are derived from your testimony in the Krajisnik case. When was it that you testified in the Krajisnik case?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot tell you the exact date. I cannot know exactly which date it was, so could the Court please look this up? I'm sure that you have all of that in your archives.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It was June 2005, if you allow me to remind you. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Possibly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: These proceedings against you were in March 2005, three months before that?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's possible that that was the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How could that report have been based on your testimony that happened three months later?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly when the report was filed, but it happened later, after I returned after having testified, that is.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I'm not really sure which report he's now referring to. If that is the real estate sale contract, I really do not see, at the moment, where that is related to the criminal charges in the document before -- that we had before on the screen, although I couldn't read it, but I don't really see that is related to the real estate sale contract. I see no basis at the moment to have the real estate sale contract be admitted. There is no relevance to it yet.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I respond?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: In terms of the accused may shed light on this, in terms of credibility, later on, in that sense we'll admit this.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1402, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In the Lower Court in Bijeljina, were you found guilty of this?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. However, I was acquitted in the appeal.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D3650. Can we have a look at the trial judgement. Can we just cast a glance at it. We can put page 1 and 2 on the ELMO, actually, because we actually do have a translation. It has arrived, but it hasn't been up-loaded. 1D3650 in e-court, please. That's the Serbian version. And on the ELMO -- we are going to place the translation on the ELMO. [In English] Could you lift it, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You see this on your screen. There is the first accused person, the second accused person, and so on. Can we have the next page, please. Number 6, they have been found guilty, all of them have been found guilty; right? [In English] Next page in English, please. "Are guilty," down there. [Interpretation] That's the judgement, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you asking me?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes, and a fine was imposed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, that will be admitted as Exhibit D1403.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And then you appealed this decision, and then you say you were acquitted of all charges; right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D3649, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So the second-instance court, the District Court in Bijeljina, does it not say the appeals of Davidovic, Milorad, and others are being dismissed? So it was dismissed, your appeal? You were not acquitted? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the first time I see this, that the fine was actually confirmed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Otherwise, fines are not something that is included in a criminal record. One does not get a criminal record on the basis of fines that are imposed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is this a criminal case?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Now everything that used to be a misdemeanor is part of criminal proceedings, because misdemeanors have been abolished altogether.
